title: Molecular basis of UV lesion binding and repair inhibition by ETS-family transcription factors.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded the structure file for 9YNZ from RCSB PDB (520,879 bytes mmCIF, 2,431 ATOM/HETATM lines) and pulled entry metadata JSON for all three deposits (9YNZ, 9OA4, 9OB0) - all three are released and freely downloadable. Read the full open-access text and its data availability statement. The supplementary archive from Europe PMC timed out twice (killed at 135 s both times), so the supplement itself is not retrievable; I only have its captions from the article text.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That Supplementary Table S1 holds crystallographic refinement statistics and Table S2 lists the molecular dynamics simulation setups; that the binding experiments used four DNA duplexes (undamaged Watson-Crick, cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer at position -2, the same lesion at -1 which becomes a T:G mismatch, and a deaminated/mismatch variant) in a single sequence context (the DPH3 gene promoter) against three ETS-family proteins (Ets1, ELF1, PU.1); and that gel images and simulation trajectories are 'available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request'.

a1_downloadable.note: Only the three co-crystal structures are public (verified: 9YNZ downloads). Every quantitative measurement - gel images for the binding and repair assays, and the molecular dynamics trajectories - is 'available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request', which is an explicit A1 failure.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: The would-be label (binding strength, or how much repair is blocked) is not a column anywhere; the numbers live inside figure panels and gel densitometry. It would have to be reconstructed by reading values off plots.

a3_inputs_present.note: Not reached in practice, but the DNA sequences and protein constructs are written out in the methods, and the structures carry full coordinates.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated clearly in the text (dissociation constants, repair rates in picomoles per minute, osmolality) - the problem is the values are not in a file, not that units are missing.

a5_enough_rows.note: Three crystal structures. The entire binding dataset is roughly four DNA duplexes times three proteins, about a dozen measured conditions in one promoter sequence context. The checklist floor is ~1,500 labelled rows (~400 for classification).

a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially small - but small because there is almost no data, which is the problem.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The three deposited structures match the three named in the data availability statement; nothing else has a count to check.

a8_label_provenance.note: The measurements are genuine physical ones (fluorescence polarization, calorimetry, gel-based repair assays), not another model's output. This killer is not the reason to reject.

existing_models.name: DeepPBS (Deep Predictor of Binding Specificity), a geometric deep-learning model for protein-DNA binding specificity, Nature Methods 2024
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported by its authors to work across protein families on both experimental and predicted protein-DNA complexes; I saw only the search abstract, so I did not read a specific number or split.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read - abstract-level search result only.

existing_models.name: Random-forest and neural-network classifiers that read UV damage patterns (CPD-seq, a method that maps UV lesions across the genome at single-base resolution) to call transcription factor binding sites - 'Mapping transcription factor binding sites by learning UV damage fingerprints', PubMed 41099699
existing_models.score_and_split: Search abstract reports 75 recovered binding sites for one yeast protein complex and 63 for another factor from as few as 6 training examples; no held-out split numbers seen.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read - abstract-level search result only.

backbone.name: None proposed - no backbone is worth naming for 3 structures and ~12 measured conditions

integration.partner_dataset: Genome-wide UV lesion maps (CPD-seq) and melanoma mutation catalogues from the same collaborating lab's earlier papers, joinable on genome coordinates
integration.join_key: genome coordinates (human genome build) plus transcription factor motif identity
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does the local DNA sequence around a transcription factor motif predict where UV lesions form and escape repair, and therefore where melanoma mutation hotspots appear - a question those genome-wide datasets could answer, but this paper's dozen biophysical measurements cannot.

controls.positive_control: Would have been: the model must recover the paper's own rank order of repair inhibition (ELF1 stronger than Ets1 stronger than PU.1) - but with one sequence context there is nothing to hold out.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is meaningless at this sample size.
controls.external_validation: None within this paper; the genome-wide CPD-seq datasets from the companion studies would be a separate project with separate data.

honest_claim_h3: With these files, the only honest claim would be about three crystal structures of one protein (PU.1) bound to four variants of a single promoter sequence - far too narrow to support any predictive statement about UV lesion binding in general.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use DNA sequence and shape around a transcription factor site to predict how UV damage changes protein binding and blocks repair.
plain_idea.train_on: Intended input: the DNA sequence of a transcription factor binding site, the position of a UV lesion within it, and the identity of the bound protein. Verified number of examples available: 3 crystal structures and roughly 12 measured protein-plus-DNA conditions.
plain_idea.predict: Intended output: binding strength (dissociation constant from fluorescence polarization) and the degree to which a repair enzyme is blocked (cleavage rate in picomoles per minute from gel assays). Both were measured in this paper but neither is published as a machine-readable table.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Skin cancer genomics groups want to know which binding sites become mutation hotspots; a working predictor would prioritise sites for sequencing. Even a failure would map how much of damage susceptibility is sequence-encoded.

more_or_better_data.why: This paper contributes 3 structures and about a dozen measured conditions in one promoter context; the models found in the search were built on genome-wide UV lesion maps and thousands of protein-DNA structures.

confidence_score.why: Triplicate measurements exist for the gel assays, which in principle gives a noise estimate, but with roughly a dozen conditions there is no way to calibrate per-prediction uncertainty.

models_beatable.why: DeepPBS is a 2024 geometric deep-learning model trained across protein families; nothing in this paper's data could be used to train a competitor, let alone beat it.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails the first condition: there is no feature-and-label table here to train on, so no baseline comparison on a shared split is possible.

ml_idea: The project considered was predicting, from DNA sequence plus lesion position, how a UV lesion changes transcription factor binding and repair accessibility. It is dead on this paper's data: the measurements are not deposited. The adjacent live idea is to use the collaborating lab's published genome-wide UV lesion maps (CPD-seq) and melanoma mutation data, which are separate deposits and would need their own evaluation.

effort.compute_note: Estimated from the one file I actually downloaded (520 KB mmCIF for 9YNZ); the three structures together are about 1.5 MB. No cross-validation is possible, so those numbers are null rather than small.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Read the data availability statement and count the deposited items: three PDB structures, with gels and simulation trajectories 'upon reasonable request'. That took two minutes and killed it.

verdict_reason: Structural paper: only 3 PDB structures public, measurements on request, no table.
